q: How does git gc decide when to run automatically and what does it prune? What risks should I know about?
answer: Git's porcelain commands that create new objects periodically check whether the repository has grown substantially since the last maintenance, and if so they invoke `git gc --auto` behind the scenes. The automatic run is triggered by two thresholds: `gc.auto` (default roughly 6700 loose objects, past which loose objects get packed) and `gc.autoPackLimit` (default 50 packs not marked with a `*.keep` file, past which packs get consolidated into one larger pack), and setting `gc.auto` to 0 disables the whole mechanism, as does setting `gc.autoPackLimit` to 0 for the pack-consolidation part. Because `gc.autoDetach` defaults to true, the auto run returns immediately and continues in the background on systems that support it, acting as a fallback when `maintenance.autoDetach` isn't set. When gc actually runs, it prunes unreachable loose objects older than a grace period—by default `prune --expire 2.weeks.ago`, plus `repack --cruft --cruft-expiration 2.weeks.ago` if cruft packs are enabled—which you can override with `gc.pruneExpire` using "now" to prune immediately or "never" to suppress pruning entirely. It is deliberately conservative about deletion, keeping anything referenced by branches, tags, the index, remote-tracking branches, reflogs, and anything else under `refs/*`, though note that a `git notes` annotation does not keep its object alive, and reflog entries themselves eventually expire (90 days by default, 30 days for entries unreachable from the current tip). The main risk is running gc concurrently with another process writing to the repository: gc may delete an object that process created but hasn't yet referenced, which can make that process fail or even corrupt the repository if it later adds a reference to the deleted object. The two-week grace period is specifically designed to mitigate this, so using `--prune=now` significantly raises the danger, and while Git has additional mitigating features, they are not a complete solution—concurrent users must accept a small (though low in practice) risk of corruption.

q: What do no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private and s-maxage mean for HTTP caches, and how is freshness determined?
answer: Freshness in HTTP caching is primarily determined by explicit expiration times that the origin server assigns using the Expires header or the max-age response directive, reflecting the server's belief that the representation will not change in a semantically significant way before that time. When no explicit expiration is present, a cache may apply a heuristic to estimate a plausible expiration time, but it must not use heuristics when an explicit time exists, and heuristics are only allowed for status codes defined as heuristically cacheable or responses explicitly marked cacheable (for example, with the public directive); a common heuristic uses the Last-Modified time, with the expiration set to no more than a fraction of the interval since that time, typically 10%. The unqualified no-cache response directive means the response must not be used to satisfy any other request without first forwarding it to the origin for validation and receiving a successful response, while the no-cache request directive similarly signals that the client prefers a stored response not be used without successful validation. The no-store directive is stricter, requiring that a cache not store any part of either the request or the response and not use the response to satisfy any other request at all. The must-revalidate response directive requires that once a response becomes stale, a cache must not reuse it until it has been successfully revalidated by the origin, and a cache must never ignore this directive—even when disconnected, it must generate an error response, typically 504 (Gateway Timeout), rather than serve the stale response. The unqualified private directive indicates the response is intended for a single user, so a shared cache must not store it, although a private (browser) cache may store it even if it would not otherwise be heuristically cacheable. Finally, s-maxage applies specifically to shared caches, specifying a maximum age that overrides whatever freshness lifetime was indicated by max-age or the Expires header. Together, these directives give origin servers and clients fine-grained control over whether responses are stored, when they must be revalidated, and how long different classes of cache may consider them fresh.
